title: Find the derivatives and antiderivatives of a range of sample functions and apply these to problems involving curve sketching, areas under curves, maxima and minima and rates of change

lessons.title: Derivatives, rates of change and tangents
lessons.html:
The derivative as a rate of change

The derivative f'(x) measures how fast f changes with respect to x. If C(t) is the cumulative grain intake at a silo in tonnes after t hours, C'(t) is the intake rate in tonnes per hour. If R(p) is revenue at price p, R'(p) shows whether a price increase raises or lowers revenue.

Rules for sample functions

  • Power rule: d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹, for any real n. So d/dx (√x) = d/dx (x^½) = ½ x^(−½).
  • Constants: d/dx (k) = 0; d/dx (k f) = k f'.
  • Sums: differentiate term by term.
  • Exponential and log: d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ; d/dx (ln x) = 1/x.

Examples

  1. f(x) = 2x³ − 6x² + 4 gives f'(x) = 6x² − 12x.
  2. g(x) = 5/x = 5x⁻¹ gives g'(x) = −5x⁻² = −5/x².

Equation of a tangent

The gradient of the tangent at x = a is f'(a). The tangent line is y − f(a) = f'(a)(x − a).

Example: f(x) = x² − 4x + 1 at x = 3. f(3) = 9 − 12 + 1 = −2. f'(x) = 2x − 4, so f'(3) = 2. Tangent: y + 2 = 2(x − 3), i.e. y = 2x − 8.

Average versus instantaneous rate

Average rate of change from x = a to x = b is [f(b) − f(a)] / (b − a), the gradient of a secant. The derivative is the limit of this as b approaches a. In practice: average intake over the day might be 40 t/h, but at 10:00 when trucks queue it might be 70 t/h.

Units matter

The units of f'(x) are units of f divided by units of x. Always state them when interpreting: "Revenue is increasing at R1,200 per R1 increase in price per bag" is meaningful; "1,200" alone is not.

lessons.title: Curve sketching, maxima and minima
lessons.html:
Using derivatives to sketch curves

For a polynomial such as f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5, the steps are:

  1. y-intercept: f(0) = 5.
  2. Stationary points: f'(x) = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −1.
  3. y-values: f(−1) = −1 − 3 + 9 + 5 = 10; f(3) = 27 − 27 − 27 + 5 = −22.
  4. Nature: f''(x) = 6x − 6. f''(−1) = −12 < 0, so (−1; 10) is a local maximum. f''(3) = 12 > 0, so (3; −22) is a local minimum.
  5. Point of inflection: f''(x) = 0 at x = 1, f(1) = −6. Concavity changes there.
  6. End behaviour: positive x³ coefficient, so f rises to the right and falls to the left.
  7. Find x-intercepts if they factorise easily, or estimate them.

Plot these points and draw a smooth curve.

Increasing and decreasing

f is increasing where f'(x) > 0 and decreasing where f'(x) < 0. Above: increasing for x < −1 and x > 3, decreasing for −1 < x < 3.

Optimisation in agri business

A farmer has 400 m of fencing to make a rectangular camp against a straight river (no fence along the river). Let the sides perpendicular to the river be x. Then the parallel side is 400 − 2x. Area A(x) = x(400 − 2x) = 400x − 2x². A'(x) = 400 − 4x = 0 gives x = 100 m. A'' = −4 < 0, so maximum. Dimensions: 100 m by 200 m, area 20,000 m² (2 ha).

Checking endpoints

On a closed interval, the absolute maximum or minimum can be at an endpoint, not only at a stationary point. Always evaluate f at the endpoints too.

lessons.title: Antiderivatives and areas under curves
lessons.html:
Antiderivatives

An antiderivative of f is any F with F' = f. The general antiderivative is written ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C.

  • ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹ / (n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1.
  • ∫ k dx = kx + C.
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln |x| + C; ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C.

Example: ∫ (6x² − 4x + 3) dx = 2x³ − 2x² + 3x + C.

Finding C from a condition

If a silo's intake rate is r(t) = 60 − 4t tonnes per hour and 0 t had been received at t = 0, then total intake C(t) = 60t − 2t² + K. C(0) = 0 gives K = 0. After 5 hours: C(5) = 300 − 50 = 250 t.

Area under a curve

For f(x) ≥ 0 on [a; b], the area between the curve and the x-axis is ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

Example: area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 3: [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = 9 − 0 = 9 square units.

If the curve dips below the x-axis, the integral counts that part as negative. To find total area, split the interval at the x-intercepts and add the absolute values.

Applications

  • Total quantity from a rate: total water pumped from a borehole when the pumping rate varies.
  • Distance from speed: a tractor's distance from its speed-time graph.
  • Total cost from marginal cost: if marginal cost is C'(x) = 20 + 0.1x rand per unit, the cost of increasing production from 100 to 200 units is ∫ from 100 to 200 of (20 + 0.1x) dx = [20x + 0.05x²] = (4,000 + 2,000) − (2,000 + 500) = R3,500.

Key points

  • The derivative gives gradient and rate of change, with units.
  • Stationary points occur where f'(x) = 0; f'' classifies them.
  • Points of inflection occur where concavity changes.
  • Check endpoints for absolute extremes.
  • Definite integrals give areas and accumulated totals.
